label: Aristotle:theorem:Stohr
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Aristotle:theorem:Stohr}
For all positive integers $h$, 
\[
n_h(2) = \left[ \frac{h^2+6h+1}{4}\right].
\]
For odd $h$, there is one extremal basis: 
\[
  \left\{0,1 , \frac{h+3}{2}  \right\}. 
\] 
For even $h$, there are two   extremal bases: 
\[
   \left\{0,1,  \frac{h}{2} + 1  \right\} \operatorname{\qquad\text{and}\qquad}   
\left\{0,1, \frac{h}{2} + 2 \right\}.   
\]
head: environment
name: St\"{o}hr

label: Aristotle:lemma:3A
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have $n \in hA$ if and only if there exist nonnegative integers 
$r_n$, $s_n$, and $t_n$  such that 
                                                               
\[
r_n + s_n + t_n  = h 
\]
and 
\[
n = r_n a + s_nb+t_nc.
\]
Then $s_n + t_n \leq h $ and 
\begin{align*}
n & = r_n a + s_nb+t_nc\\
&  = (r_n + s_n + t_n)a + s_n(b-a) +t_n(c-a) \\
& = ha + s_nx +t_ny.
\end{align*}
Thus, $n \in hA$ implies~\eqref{Aristotle:3Aineq} and~\eqref{Aristotle:3Asum}. 

Conversely, if conditions~\eqref{Aristotle:3Aineq} and~\eqref{Aristotle:3Asum} are
satisfied, then 
\[
r_n = h-s_n-t_n \in \ensuremath{ \mathbf N }_0
\]
 and 
\begin{align*}
n & = ha + s_nx +t_ny  \\ 
& =  (r_n + s_n + t_n)a + s_n(b-a) + t_n(c-a) \\
& = r_n a + s_nb+t_nc \in hA. 
\end{align*}
Thus,~\eqref{Aristotle:3Aineq} and~\eqref{Aristotle:3Asum} imply $n \in hA$.
This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: Aristotle:lemma:xya
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have $[0,h+1] \subseteq hA$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Aristotle:lemma:3A}, for all $n \in [0,h+1]$ there exist 
$s_n,t_n \in [0,h]$ such that $s_n+t_n \leq h$ and 
\[
n = ha+s_nx+t_ny.
\] 
By the pigeonhole principle, there exist $n_1,n_2$ with $0 \leq n_1 < n_2 \leq h+1$ 
and $s_{n_1} = s_{n_2}$.  Then $t_{n_1} < t_{n_2}$ and 
\[
h+1 \geq n_2-n_1 = \left( t_{n_2} - t_{n_1}\right) y \geq y.
\] 
This proves~\eqref{Aristotle:xya-y}.

We have 
\[
0 = ha + s_0 x + t_0 y \in hA
\] 
and 
\[
1 = ha + s_1 x + t_1 y \in hA
\] 
Subtracting, we obtain  
\[
1 = (s_1 - s_0)x + (t_1 - t_0)y
\]
and so
\[
\gcd(x,y)=1.
\]
This proves~\eqref{Aristotle:xya-gcd}.

Because  $h+1\in hA$ and $y \leq h+1$, we have  
\[
h+1= ha +s_{h+1}x+t_{h+1}y \leq ha + (s_{h+1}+t_{h+1})y \leq ha + h(h+1) 
\] 
and so 
\[
a \geq -h-1+  \frac{h+1}{h}  = -\left(h - \frac{1}{h}\right).
\]
Because $a$ is an integer, we have $a \geq  -(h-1)$. 
This proves~\eqref{Aristotle:xya-a}. 

For all $n \in hA$ we have  
\[
n= ha +s_nx+t_ny \leq  ha + h(h+1) 
\] 
and 
\[
a \geq -h-1 + \frac{n}{h}. 
\]
This proves~\eqref{Aristotle:xya-n}.
head: environment

label: Aristotle:lemma:algorithm
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Aristotle:lemma:algorithm}
Let $h \geq 3$.  Then $n^{\flat}_h(2)$ 
is the maximum of $n_h(A)$ for all sets $A = \{a,a+x,a+y\}$ 
such that 
\[
1 \leq x < y \leq h+1, \qquad \gcd(x,y) = 1,
\]
and 
\[
-(h-1) \leq a \leq -1.
\]
The number of sets $A$ satisfying these conditions is
\[
(h-1)\sum_{y=2}^{h+1}\varphi(y) \leq (h-1)\binom{h+1}{2}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $h \geq 3$ and $A = \{-1,0,2\}$.  Then 
\[
n^{\flat}_h(2) \geq n_h(A) \geq 2h-2 \geq h+1.   
\] 
Thus, to compute $n^{\flat}_h(2)$, it suffices to compute $n_h(A)$
only for sets $A$ such that $[0,h+1] \subseteq hA$.  
The result now follows directly from Lemma~\ref{Aristotle:lemma:xya}.
head: environment

label: Aristotle:theorem:new
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Aristotle:theorem:new}
For all positive integers $h$, 
\[
n^{\flat}_h(2) \leq n_h(2) = \left[ \frac{h^2 +6h + 1}{4} \right].
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For even $h$, consider the sets  
\[
A_1 = \left\{0,1,\frac{h}{2}+1\right\} \operatorname{\qquad\text{and}\qquad} A_2 = \left\{0,1,\frac{h}{2}+2\right\}.
\]
The sumset $hA_1$ contains the set 
\begin{align*} 
\left[ 0, \frac{h^2+6h}{4} \right] 
& = 
\left\{ \left(\frac{h}{2}+1\right)q+r: q \in \left[0,\frac{h}{2} \right]  
\text{ and } r \in  \left[0,\frac{h}{2} \right]   \right\} \\
&  \qquad  \cup \left\{ \left(\frac{h}{2}+1\right)^2+r: 
 r \in  \left[0,\frac{h}{2} -1\right]   \right\}
\end{align*}
and 
\[
\frac{h^2+6h}{4} +1 \notin hA_1.
\]
Therefore, 
\[
n_h(A_1) = \frac{h^2 +6h}{4}.
\]

The sumset $hA_2$ contains the set 
\begin{align*} 
\left[ 0, \frac{h^2+6h}{4} \right] 
& = 
\left\{ \left(\frac{h}{2}+2\right)q+r: q \in \left[0,\frac{h}{2} - 1\right]  
\text{ and } r \in  \left[0,\frac{h}{2} +1\right]   \right\} \\
& \qquad \cup \left\{ \left(\frac{h}{2}+2\right) \frac{h}{2}+r: 
 r \in  \left[0,\frac{h}{2}  \right]   \right\}
\end{align*}
and 
\[
\frac{h^2+6h}{4} +1 \notin hA_2.
\]
Therefore, 
\[
n_h(A_2) = \frac{h^2 +6h}{4}.   
\]

For odd $h$, consider the set   
\[
A_3 = \left\{0,1,\frac{h+3}{2} \right\}.
\]
The sumset $hA_3$ contains the set 
\begin{align*} 
\left[ 0, \frac{h^2+6h+1}{4} \right] 
& = 
\left\{ \left(\frac{h+3}{2} \right)q+r: q \in \left[0,\frac{h-1}{2} \right]  
\text{ and } r \in  \left[0,\frac{h+1}{2} \right]   \right\} \\
& \qquad \cup \left\{ \left(\frac{h+3}{2} \right) \left( \frac{h+1}{2} \right) +r: 
 r \in  \left[0,\frac{h-1}{2}  \right]   \right\}
\end{align*}
and 
\[
\frac{h^2+6h+1}{4} +1 \notin hA_3.
\]
Therefore, 
\[
n_h(A_3) = \frac{h^2 +6h+1}{4}.
\]
It follows that 
\begin{equation}        \label{Aristotle:nhA-ineq}
n_h(2) \geq \left[ \frac{h^2 +6h + 1}{4} \right] 
\end{equation} 
for all positive integers $h$. 
We shall prove that, for all sets $A \in \binom{\ensuremath{\mathbf Z}}{3}$,   
\begin{equation}        \label{Aristotle:nhA-ineq-2}
n_h(A) \leq \left[ \frac{h^2+6h+1}{4} \right].
\end{equation}

Let $A = \{a,b,c\}$ with $a < b < c$ and let $x = b-a$ and $y = c-a$.  
Inequality~\eqref{Aristotle:nhA-ineq-2} holds if $n_h(A) \leq h$.  
Thus, we can assume that 
\[
N = n_h(A) \geq h+1.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{Aristotle:lemma:xya}, 
\[
y \leq h+1
\operatorname{\qquad\text{and}\qquad}
\gcd(x,y) = 1.
\]
Consider the congruence class $ha-x \pmod{y}$. There exist unique integers 
\[
n_3 \in [0,y-1] \operatorname{\qquad\text{and}\qquad} n_4 \in [N-y+1,N]
\]
such that 
\[
n_3 \equiv n_4 \equiv ha-x \pmod{y}.
\]
Then $n_3,n_4 \in hA$ and 
\begin{equation}                  \label{Aristotle:n3n4ineq}
n_4 - n_3  \geq (N-y+1) - (y-1) = N - 2y + 2. 
\end{equation}
\begin{samepage}
The congruence
\[
n_3 = ha+s_{n_3}x+ t_{n_3}y \equiv ha+s_{n_3}x  \equiv ha-x \pmod{y}
\]
implies  
\[
(s_{n_3} +1)x  \equiv 0 \pmod{y}.
\]
\end{samepage}
From $\gcd(x,y)=1$, we obtain  
\[
s_{n_3} \equiv -1 \pmod{y}. 
\]
Then $s_{n_3} \geq 0$ implies  
\[
s_{n_3} \geq y-1
\]
and 
\[
n_3 \geq ha + s_{n_3}x \geq  ha +(y-1)x. 
\]
Similarly, 
\[
s_{n_4} \geq y-1.
\]
The inequality $t_{n_4} \leq h-s_{n_4}$ implies 
\begin{align*}
n_4 & = ha + s_{n_4}x + t_{n_4}y \\
& \leq ha + s_{n_4}x + (h-s_{n_4}) y \\
& = ha + hy - s_{n_4}(y-x) \\
& \leq ha + hy -  (y-1) (y-x).
\end{align*}
Therefore, 
\begin{align*}
n_4 - n_3 
& \leq (ha + hy -  (y-1) (y-x)) - (ha +(y-1)x ) \\
& = hy - y^2 + y. 
\end{align*}
Applying inequality~\eqref{Aristotle:n3n4ineq} gives
\[
N - 2y + 2 \leq n_4 - n_3 \leq hy - y^2 + y 
\]
and so 
\begin{align*}
n_h(A) = N & \leq - y^2 + (h+3)y -2 \\ 
& = \frac{h^2+6h+1}{4} - \left(y-\left(\frac{h+3}{2}\right)\right)^2 \\
& \leq \frac{h^2+6h+1}{4}. 
\end{align*}
From inequality~\eqref{Aristotle:nhA-ineq},
for every 3-element set $A$ of integers, we have  
\[
n_h(A) \leq \left[ \frac{h^2+6h+1}{4} \right] \leq n_h(2). 
\]
It follows that 
\[
n_h(2) \leq  \left[ \frac{h^2+6h+1}{4} \right] \leq n_h(2)
\]
and
\[
n^{\flat}_h(2) \leq  \left[ \frac{h^2+6h+1}{4} \right] = n_h(2). 
\]
This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: Aristotle:theorem:h=4
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Aristotle:theorem:h=4}
For $h=4$, 
\[
n^{\flat}_4(2) = 8 < 10 = n_4(2).
\] 
The extremal bases for $n_4(2)$ are 
\[
 \{0,1,3\} \operatorname{\qquad\text{and}\qquad} \{0,1,4\}.
\] 
The extremal bases for $n^{\flat}_4(2)$ are 
\[
\{-3,1,2\}, \quad \{-2,1,2\}, \quad \{-2,1,3\}, \quad \{-1,1,2\}, \quad \{-1,1,4\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
From Theorem~\ref{Aristotle:theorem:Stohr} we obtain $n_4(2) = 10$ 
and the extremal bases for $n_4(2)$. 
From Theorem~\ref{Aristotle:theorem:new} we obtain $n^{\flat}_4(2) \leq 10$. 

Let $A = \{a, b, c\}$ be a set of integers with $a <  b < c$ and $a < 0$.  
Setting $x=b-a$ and $y = c-a$, we have $A = \{a,a+x,a+y\}$. 
If $[0,8] \subseteq 4A$, then inequalities~\eqref{Aristotle:xya-y} 
and~\eqref{Aristotle:xya-n} from 
Lemma~\ref{Aristotle:lemma:xya} with $h = 4$ and $n = 8$ give  
\[
1 \leq x < y \leq 5
\]
and
\[
-1 \geq a \geq -5 + \frac{8}{4} = -3.
\]
There are $3\binom{5}{2} = 30$ sets $A  = \{a,a+x,a+y\}$ 
that satisfy these conditions.  
Computer calculation (using Maple) shows that $n_4(A) \leq 8$ 
for each of these 30 sets and that $n_4(A) = 8$ for the five sets 
listed in the statement of Theorem~\ref{Aristotle:theorem:h=4}.
Therefore, $n^{\flat}_4(2) = 8$. 
This completes the proof.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Writing 
\[
h = 4w-2
\]
we have  
\[
n_h(2) = \frac{h^2+6h}{4} = (w+1)h.
\]
Let 
\[
A = \{-w,w,w+1\} = -w + \{0,2w,2w+1\}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{Aristotle:lemma:3A}, 
\begin{align*}
hA & = -hw + \left\{ 2ws + (2w+1)t: s,t \in \ensuremath{ \mathbf N }_0 \text{ and } s+t \leq h \right\} \\
& = -hw + \bigcup_{\ell=0}^h \left\{ 2ws + (2w+1)t: s,t \in \ensuremath{ \mathbf N }_0 \text{ and } s+t = \ell  \right\} \\
& = -hw + \bigcup_{\ell=0}^h \left\{ 2w\ell + t : t \in [0,\ell] \right\} \\
& = -hw + \bigcup_{\ell=0}^h [2w\ell , (2w + 1)\ell].
\end{align*}
We have 
\[
2w(\ell  +1) \leq 2w\ell + \ell + 1 
\] 
if and only if 
\[
\ell \geq 2w-1
\]
and so 
\begin{align*}
hA 
&  = \left(-hw + \bigcup_{\ell=0}^{2w-2} [2w\ell, (2w + 1)\ell] \right)
\cup \left(-hw + \bigcup_{\ell=2w-1}^h [2w\ell, (2w + 1)\ell] \right) \\
&  = \left(-hw + \bigcup_{\ell=0}^{2w-2} [2w\ell, (2w + 1)\ell] \right)
\cup \left(-hw + [2w(2w-1), (2w + 1)h] \right) \\
&  = \left(-hw + \bigcup_{\ell=0}^{2w-2} [2w\ell, (2w + 1)\ell] \right)
\cup   [0, (w + 1)h]  \\
& \supseteq [0, n_h(2)],
\end{align*}
and so $n_h(2) = n_h(A) \leq n^{\flat}_h(2) \leq n_h(2)$.  
This completes the proof.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Writing 
\[
h = 4w
\]
we have $w \geq 2$ and 
\[
n_h(2) = \frac{h^2+6h}{4} = w(4w+6).
\]
Let 
\[
A = \{-(w-1),w,w+2\} = -(w-1)+ \{0,2w-1,2w+1\}.
\]
Note that if $h=4$, then $w=1$ and the set $A = \{0,1,3\}$ 
contains no negative integer. 

By Lemma~\ref{Aristotle:lemma:3A}, 
\begin{align*}
hA & = -h(w-1) + \left\{ (2w-1)s + (2w+1)t: s,t \in \ensuremath{ \mathbf N }_0 \text{ and } s+t \leq h \right\} \\
& = -h(w-1) + \bigcup_{\ell=0}^h \left\{ (2w-1)s + (2w+1)t: s,t \in \ensuremath{ \mathbf N }_0 \text{ and } s+t = \ell  \right\} \\
& =  -h(w-1) + \bigcup_{\ell=0}^h \left\{ (2w-1)\ell + 2t : t \in [0,\ell] \right\} \\
& =  -h(w-1) + \bigcup_{\ell=0}^h   [(2w-1)\ell, (2w+1)\ell]_{\ell\pmod{2}}.
\end{align*}
The set $ [(2w-1)\ell, (2w+1)\ell]_{\ell\pmod{2}}$ is 
a sequence of $\ell+1$ consecutive even integers if $\ell$ is even and 
a sequence of $\ell+1$ consecutive odd integers if $\ell$ is odd. 
We have 
\[
(2w-1)(\ell  +2) \leq (2w+1)\ell + 2 
\] 
if and only if 
\[
2w-2 \leq \ell.
\]
Because $h$ is even, we have 
\begin{align*}
 -h(w-1) +&   \bigcup_{\substack{\ell=2w-2 \\ \ell \equiv 0 \pmod{2}}}^h 
  [(2w-1)\ell, (2w+1)\ell]_{0\pmod{2}} \\
& =  -h(w-1) +  [(2w-1)(2w-2), (2w+1)h]_{\text{even}} \\
& =   [-2(w-1), (w+2)h]_{\text{even}} \\
& \supseteq [-2(w-1), n_h(2)]_{\text{even}}
\end{align*}
and 
\begin{align*}
 -h(w-1) &+  \bigcup_{\substack{\ell=2w-1 \\ \ell \equiv 1 \pmod{2}}}^{h-1} 
  [(2w-1)\ell, (2w+1)\ell]_{1 \pmod{2}}\\
& =  -h(w-1) + [(2w-1)(2w-1), (2w+1)(h-1)]_{\text{odd}} \\
& = [1, -h(w-1)+(2w+1)(h-1)]_{\text{odd}} \\
& =    [1,n_h(2)-1]_{\text{odd}}. 
\end{align*}
Therefore,
\[
hA \supseteq [0,n_h(2)]
\]
and $n_h(2) \geq n^{\flat}_h(2) \geq n_h(A)$. 
This completes the proof.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is straightforward to check that  
\[
n^{\flat}_1(2) = 1 < 2 = n_1(2) 
\]
and that $\{0,1,2\}$ is  the unique extremal set for $n_1(2)$.   
The extremal sets for $n^{\flat}_1(2)$ are the sets $\{a, 0,1\}$ for 
all  integers $a < 0$.  

Let $h = 2m+1 \geq 3$.  
By Theorem~\ref{Aristotle:theorem:new}, 
\[
n^{\flat}_h(2)  \leq n_h(2) =  \frac{h^2 + 6h +1}{4} = m^2 + 4m + 2  = N
\]
and $h+1 \leq N$.  
If $n^{\flat}_h(2) = n_h(2)$, then there is a set $A = \{a,b,c\}$ with 
$a <   b < c$ and $a < 0$ such that 
\[
[0,h+1] \subseteq [0, N] \subseteq hA. 
\]
Let $x = b-a$ and $y = c-a$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Aristotle:lemma:xya}, 
\[
A = \{a,b,c\} = a + \{0,x,y\}
\] 
with 
\[
1 \leq x < y \leq h+1
\]
and 
\[
\gcd(x,y) = 1.
\]
By  Lemma~\ref{Aristotle:lemma:3A}, we have 
$n \in hA$ if and only if there exist  integers $s_n \in [0,h]$ 
and $t_n \in [0,h]$ such that 
\[
s_n + t_n \leq h
\]
and 
\begin{equation}         \label{Aristotle:sntn}
n = ha + s_n x + t_ny.
\end{equation}

Consider the congruence class $ha-x \pmod{y}$. 
There are unique integers 
\[
n_3 \in [0,y-1] \operatorname{\qquad\text{and}\qquad} n_4 \in [N-y+1,N]
\]
such that 
\[
n_3 \equiv n_4 \equiv ha-x \pmod{y}. 
\]
Representing $n_3$ and $n_4$ in the form~\eqref{Aristotle:sntn}, 
we obtain
\[
n_4-n_3 \equiv (s_{n_4} - s_{n_3})x \equiv 0 \pmod{y} 
\]
and so 
\[
s_{n_4} \equiv  s_{n_3} \pmod{y}.
\]
We also have 
\[
n_3 \equiv ha + s_{n_3}x \equiv ha-x \pmod{y}
\]
and so
\[
(s_{n_3}+1)x \equiv 0 \pmod{y}.
\]
Therefore, 
\[
s_{n_3} \equiv -1 \pmod{y}.
\]
Because $s_{n_3} \geq 0$, we have 
\[
                                            
s_{n_3} \geq y-1. 
\] 
Then 
\[
y - 1 \geq n_3 = ha + s_{n_3}x + t_{n_3}y \geq ha +s_{n_3}x  \geq ha + (y-1) x 
\] 
and so 
\begin{equation}                  \label{Aristotle:upper-ha}
ha \leq (y-1) - (y-1)x = (y-1)(1-x) = U.
\end{equation} 

Similarly, 
\[
                                            
s_{n_4} \geq y-1. 
\]
We have $t_{n_4} \leq h-s_{n_4}$ and 
\begin{align*} 
N - y + 1 & \leq 
n_4   = ha + s_{n_4}x + t_{n_4}y \\
& \leq ha + s_{n_4}x + ( h-s_{n_4}) y \\ 
& = ha +hy -  s_{n_4} (y-x)  \\ 
& \leq ha +hy - (y-1)(y-x)  
\end{align*} 
and so 
\begin{equation}                  \label{Aristotle:lower-ha}
ha \geq N- hy + (y-1)(y-x-1) = L.
\end{equation}
Combining inequalities~\eqref{Aristotle:upper-ha} 
and~\eqref{Aristotle:lower-ha}, we obtain 
\[
U = (y-1)(1-x) \geq N - hy + (y-1)(y-x - 1) = L                                       
\] 
or 
\[
0 \geq L-U = N - hy + (y-1)(y-2).
\]
Recalling that $h = 2m+1$ and $N = m^2 + 4m + 2$, we obtain 
\begin{align*}
0 & \geq L - U = N - hy + (y-1)(y-2)  \\
& = (m^2+4m+2) -(2m+1)y+y^2-3y+2 \\
& = (m-y)^2 +4(m-y)+4\\
& = (m-y+2)^2 \\ 
& \geq 0. 
\end{align*}  
\begin{samepage}
Therefore,
\[
y = m + 2 
\]
and 
\[
 ha = U =  (y-1)(1-x) =  (m+1)(1-x) < 0. 
\]
\end{samepage}
It follows that $1-x < 0$ and so 
\[
1 \leq x -1 \leq y - 2 = m.
\]
Also, 
\[
2ha = 2(m+1)(1-x) = (h+1)(1-x) = h(1-x)+1-x
\]
implies 
\[
(2m+1)(2a+x-1) = h(2a+x-1) = -(x-1)
\]
and so $2m+1$ divides the integer $x-1$ in $[1,m]$, which is absurd.
Therefore, $n^{\flat}_h(2) < n_h(2)$. 
This completes the proof.
head: environment
